tldr: We present a humanoid locomotion control method that continuously adapts from perceptive to blind walking by always fusing a learned denoising world model with a proprioceptive encoder, even when camera depth images suffer from partial noise and occlusions.
hero_caption: Comparison of locomotion paradigms for legged robots: (a) blind locomotion relying solely on proprioception, (b)(c) perceptive locomotion assuming clean depth images, (d) binary switching between perception and blind control based on confidence, and (e) the proposed CAP, which continuously co-activates and fuses a denoising world model and proprioception.
overview:
Humanoids traversing complex terrains like stairs and obstacles require exteroceptive depth sensing to anticipate the path ahead. In the real world, however, depth images frequently become corrupted due to motion blur from intense shaking, limb occlusions, and sensor dropouts. Conventional perceptive policies assume that depth observations remain clean and in-distribution, quickly failing when images degrade. Meanwhile, prior attempts that prepare separate perceptive and blind (proprioception-only) policies switch between them in a binary manner. A major flaw with this setup is that even slight noise triggers a switch to the blind policy, discarding recoverable, useful terrain information remaining in the partially corrupted image.

To address this, the authors introduce CAP (Continuously Adaptive Perception-Blind Policy), a single-stage policy that continuously adapts along a spectrum from perceptive to blind control depending on the degree of noise. At its core is a dual-path architecture combining a perceptive world-model encoder—trained as a learned denoiser to reconstruct clean terrain from corrupted depth—and a proprioceptive VAE that captures high-frequency body states. During training, a coupled recipe pairs a depth-noise curriculum on the input with world-model feature dropout on the policy-facing latent space. As a result, the robot gracefully degrades to blind locomotion only when vision is completely lost, while continuing to denoise inputs and anticipate upcoming obstacles under partial corruption.

In Isaac Gym simulations with the Unitree G1, CAP matches or outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under clean, informative conditions. Across an 8-level sensor quality sweep, it demonstrates graceful degradation rather than the abrupt performance cliff seen in binary-switching baselines. Furthermore, deployments on the physical Unitree G1 show robust, uninterrupted locomotion under manual camera occlusions during walking, sensor saturation from flashlight glare, and outdoor depth artifacts on grass.
contributions: Proposed CAP, a single-stage locomotion policy that eliminates binary switching between perception and blind control by continuously fusing a depth-denoising world model with a proprioceptive encoder.

Introduced a coupled training recipe combining an input-level depth-noise curriculum and latent-level feature dropout, achieving graceful degradation across corruption patterns ranging from partial noise to complete visual loss.

Demonstrated zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree G1, maintaining stable walking under manual camera occlusion, outdoor depth dropouts on grass, and sensor washout from external flashes.

sections.heading: Should robots really switch to blind walking whenever depth gets noisy?
sections.summary: Real-world humanoid walking frequently suffers from partial depth corruption and blur. Because neither clean-depth perceptive policies nor binary-switching methods handle intermediate noise well, this paper introduces CAP to recover terrain information from corrupted inputs and smoothly fuse vision with proprioception.
sections.details:
For humanoids to tackle unstructured terrains like stairs, gaps, and hurdles, they cannot merely react to contact forces; forward-looking exteroception (such as depth cameras) is vital to anticipate obstacles. Yet in the physical world, depth observations are routinely degraded by motion blur from rapid dynamics, self-occlusions, and intermittent packet drops. Crucially, real sensor failures are rarely strictly binary. Most of the time, perception lies on a continuous spectrum where depth is partially corrupted but still carries valuable terrain information.

Prior studies have approached this challenge from two extremes:
- Blind policies: Immune to visual sensor noise because they rely exclusively on proprioception, but unable to foresee upcoming gaps or drop-offs.
- Perceptive policies: Fully trust depth images as clean observations, leading to rapid failure when out-of-distribution corruption occurs.
- Switching-based systems: Route between separate perceptive and blind sub-policies. However, even moderate noise often triggers the fallback to blind control, completely discarding recoverable geometric clues in the image and risking jerky control transitions.

CAP fills this middle ground with a unified policy. It runs a world-model encoder that reconstructs clean terrain from corrupted depth concurrently with a high-frequency proprioceptive encoder, fusing their latent features at all times. This setup denoises observations to maintain forward anticipation under partial corruption, smoothly falling back to blind locomotion only under extreme, unrecoverable conditions.

sections.heading: Why binary switching between vision and blindness falls short
sections.summary: Previous works bridging blind and perceptive walking often relied on arbiters or gating between separate sub-policies. However, they were designed around falling back to blind control whenever vision degraded, overlooking the potential to actively denoise and exploit corrupted visual inputs.
sections.details:
### Blind vs. Perceptive Locomotion in Legged Robots
Blind walking reacts to ground contact forces and handles uneven ground well, but it cannot proactively clear high ledges or wide gaps. To overcome this, researchers explored building 2.5D elevation maps from LiDAR or feeding raw camera depth straight into end-to-end perceptive policies. Extensions like PIE reconstruct elevation maps via auxiliary tasks, while WMP incorporates world-model autoencoders. Nevertheless, these methods implicitly assume clean, in-distribution depth inputs, failing under sustained sensor corruption.

### Paradigms for Fusing Vision and Proprioception
Recently, several works arbitrate between perceptive and blind sub-policies (such as VB-Com, MBC, and RENet). They switch policies based on reconstruction errors or value function estimates. Yet, their fundamental philosophy remains routing around perception when it looks unreliable. They discard the opportunity to recover usable geometry from partially corrupted depth.

Figure F2 highlights how CAP departs from these paradigms. CAP avoids either-or switching. Instead, it keeps its denoising world model and proprioceptive encoder co-active at all times. Under mild to moderate noise, it reconstructs clean terrain in latent space to negotiate obstacles, smoothly fading into proprioception-dominant control only when vision is entirely lost.

captions.F2: Comparison of locomotion paradigms and CAP: (a) proprioception-only blind control, (b) perceptive control directly using raw depth, (c) PIE with elevation map reconstruction, (d) Binary-switch selecting policies via reconstruction error, and (e) CAP, which continuously fuses latent representations from a denoising world model and a proprioceptive VAE.

sections.heading: Inside CAP: World-model denoising and dual-path fusion
sections.summary: CAP is a single policy combining a low-frequency (10Hz) world model that reconstructs a clean, gravity-aligned perspective from corrupted depth with a high-frequency (50Hz) proprioceptive VAE. A coupled training recipe pairing input noise with latent dropout ensures smooth adaptation down to complete visual loss.
sections.details:
### 3.1 System Overview and Asymmetric Actor-Critic
CAP is trained in a single stage using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The actor policy receives only deployable observations: a proprioceptive vector $o_t$ and forward depth image $d_t$. In contrast, the critic leverages privileged simulation states, including base linear velocity $v_t$, disturbance force $e_t$, and ground-truth local elevation map $m_t$. The actor's input layer employs a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE, $K=4$ experts) with a shared gating network to weight and fuse visual and proprioceptive representations.

### 3.2 Dual-Path Architecture with Complementary Encoders
Two encoders operate concurrently across different modalities and timescales:
- Perceptive World-Model (WM) Encoder (10Hz): Built on the DreamerV3 Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM). Its deterministic hidden state $h_t$ is projected by an MLP into a 32-dimensional latent vector $z^{\text{wm}}_t$. Critically, the reconstruction target is decoupled from the input: the input is a noisy depth image $d_t$ pitched and rolled with the robot body, while the reconstruction target $d_t^{\mathrm{tgt}}$ is clean, ground-truth depth rendered from a gravity-aligned, pitch-and-roll-neutralized camera pose. This forces the encoder to simultaneously denoise and remove body-tilt artifacts, learning a stabilized terrain representation.
- Proprioceptive VAE Encoder (50Hz): A $\beta$-VAE that extracts a 16-dimensional body-state latent vector $z^{\text{vae}}_t$ from a 5-step proprioceptive history $o_t^H$. This fast, depth-free path anchors body state estimation and prevents the policy from drifting due to world-model overshooting during prolonged visual outages.

### 3.3 Coupled Training Recipe for Graceful Degradation
To endure severe real-world corruptions, two coupled mechanisms are introduced:
- Depth-Noise Curriculum: Synthesizes five noise types—Gaussian noise, salt-and-pepper noise, partial rectangular occlusions, edge occlusions, and full blackouts. Corruption severity $n_e$ scales adaptively with individual environment success rates.
- World-Model Feature Dropout: With probability $p_e$ tied to noise severity $n_e$, the latent vector $z^{\text{wm}}_t$ fed to the actor is perturbed by zeroing it out (loss), adding Gaussian noise (distortion), or swapping it with latents from another environment (inconsistency). This prevents the actor from over-relying on the world model and ignoring proprioception, ensuring it remains robust even under complete visual failure.

sections.heading: Simulation and real-world trials: Can it walk through mounting noise?
sections.summary: In simulation, CAP matched high success rates under clean conditions while degrading far more smoothly than binary switching as noise worsened. On the physical Unitree G1, it smoothly handled manual camera occlusions, external camera flashes, and outdoor grass walking without stumbling.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Simulation Setup and Baseline Comparison
Evaluations were conducted on the Unitree G1 in Isaac Gym across four challenging terrains: Stairs, Platforms, Gaps, and Hurdles. Baselines included Hiking (perceptive without denoising), PIE (elevation map reconstruction), and Binary-switch (threshold-based switching between perceptive and blind policies).

Under clean depth ('Clean') and severe noise ('Noisy') conditions (Table 1), CAP demonstrated remarkable robustness, achieving a 99.6% average success rate on Clean and 97.9% on Noisy. Hiking collapsed under noise, and PIE suffered steep performance drops. While Binary-switch climbed stairs blindly, it fell immediately on Platforms and Gaps the moment it switched to blind control, as visual foresight is indispensable there.

Ablation studies confirmed:
- Removing MoE (-MoE): Degraded performance across both Clean and Noisy setups, most noticeably on stairs.
- Removing the noise curriculum (-noise curr.): Preserved Clean performance but crippled resilience under Noisy conditions.
- Removing the VAE encoder (-VAE encoder): Caused consistent performance drops in both settings, proving that proprioceptive encoding is essential at all times, not just as a fallback.

### 4.2 Visual Quality Sweep: Validating Continuous Adaptation
In an 8-level sweep degrading depth quality from clean to complete loss, Binary-switch dropped off a cliff at a specific threshold. In contrast, CAP showed a remarkably gentle decline. On vision-critical terrains, it squeezed out every bit of remaining geometric signal; on blind-traversable terrains like stairs, it smoothly settled into stable blind walking baselines.

### 4.3 Real-World Unitree G1 Deployment
The policy was deployed zero-shot on an onboard Jetson Orin with an Intel RealSense D435i mounted on the G1's head.
- Manual Occlusion Tests (Fig. F4 a): A cardboard sheet completely covered the camera mid-ascent and was subsequently removed. The robot ascended the stairs blindly and, upon unmasking, immediately re-acquired the forward gap to leap across it, achieving a seamless recovery (39/40 successful indoor trials).
- Sensor Disturbance Tests (Fig. F4 b, c): When a high-intensity flashlight caused widespread visual washout and sensor saturation, the world model denoised and recovered the footholds, allowing uninterrupted walking. CAP also crossed outdoor platforms, stairs, and grass with severe depth dropouts absent from simulation.

captions.F4: Real-world trials on the Unitree G1: (a) uninterrupted walking during manual camera occlusion and release on stairs, (b) traversing terrain under flashlight-induced sensor saturation, and (c) outdoor trials across platforms, grass, and stairs. Inset images show raw depth (red border, left) alongside denoised world-model reconstructions (green border, right).

sections.heading: Conclusions and future directions: Toward safety at the perception boundary
sections.summary: CAP demonstrates that continuously blending a denoising world model with proprioception produces a robust locomotion policy under perceptual degradation. Future work must address severe camera misalignment and incorporate active safety stops or recovery behaviors when vision is lost on vision-critical terrains.
sections.details:
### Conclusion
This paper presented CAP, moving beyond binary switching to achieve continuously adaptive humanoid locomotion under perceptual noise. By combining a learned denoising world model, a high-frequency proprioceptive VAE, and a coupled curriculum of input noise and latent feature dropout, CAP achieves graceful degradation across the entire spectrum from partial noise to complete visual blackout.

### Limitations and Future Work
The authors point out two key limitations:
- Tolerance to Large Geometric Distortions: Out-of-distribution extrinsic errors, such as physical camera mount shifts, can distort the reconstructed terrain representation.
- Safety on Vision-Critical Terrains: When exteroception fails completely before a wide gap, merely degrading to blind walking cannot prevent a fall. Future systems should incorporate active confidence estimation, risk-aware policy selection to stop before hazards, and protective recovery maneuvers after missteps.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details and why feature dropout matters
sections.summary: The appendix details the multithreaded real-time implementation decoupling the 10Hz world model from the 50Hz control loop, and provides stroboscopic evidence showing how latent feature dropout eliminates visual overshooting when stepping off stairs.
sections.details:
### Real-Time Asynchronous Architecture
On the physical G1, the computationally demanding world model (10Hz) runs asynchronously from the high-frequency actor/VAE control loop (50Hz) via multithreading. Latents produced by the world model are written to a thread-safe buffer, which the 50Hz policy reads at each step. Running via ONNX Runtime, policy inference latency stays around 2ms, preventing any jitter in the low-level control loop.

### Impact of World-Model Feature Dropout (Fig. F5)
Appendix B.5 evaluates what happens when vision is fully occluded as the robot steps off stairs onto flat ground:
- Without Feature Dropout (Fig. F5 b): The world model clings to its recent memory of climbing and erroneously predicts that stairs continue ahead (overshooting). Consequently, the robot performs unnecessary high-stepping motions (red boxes) for two full steps on flat ground.
- With Feature Dropout (CAP, Fig. F5 a): Having learned during training that visual latents can be uninformative, the policy quickly trusts foot-contact proprioception, returning to normal flat-ground walking (green box) after just one exploratory step.

captions.F5: Stroboscopic comparison of stair-to-flat transitions under complete camera occlusion. Red boxes indicate high-stepping overshoot onto flat ground; green boxes indicate recovery to normal gait. (a) CAP with feature dropout recovers after one step, whereas (b) CAP without dropout overshoots for two steps due to world-model hallucination.
captions.F6: Additional real-world deployment experiments on the Unitree G1: (a)-(c) indoor occlusion trials across stairs, platforms, and mixed terrains; (d)-(f) out-of-distribution outdoor environments, including curb edges, outdoor staircases, and grass with severe depth artifacts.

takeaways: Rather than binary switching between vision and blindness, continuously blending denoised visual latents with proprioception provides the strongest defense against imperfect real-world sensors.
Using clean, gravity-aligned depth as the world model's reconstruction target enables a single encoder to both denoise depth and neutralize robot body oscillations.
Deliberately dropping out visual latent features during training prevents world-model hallucination and overshooting during visual dropouts, allowing proprioception to ground the policy.
limitations: Large out-of-distribution geometric shifts, such as physical camera displacement or calibration drift, can corrupt the denoised terrain reconstruction.
When vision is completely lost on vision-critical terrains like deep gaps, falling back to blind control cannot prevent a drop; active stopping and safety recovery behaviors remain to be integrated.
